claims.claim: In a study of nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease in long-term care, mean food intake was 25% higher and mean liquid intake 84% higher with high-contrast red tableware than with white tableware, and 8 of 9 men increased their intake.
claims.supporting_passage: Participants were nine men with advanced AD. ... Data were collected for 30 days (10 days per condition) for two meals per day. White tableware was used for the baseline and post-intervention conditions, and high-contrast red tableware for the intervention condition. ... Mean percent increase was 25% for food and 84% for liquid for the high-contrast intervention (red) versus baseline (white) condition, with 8 of 9 participants exhibiting increased intake. [Gaffney 2026, Limitations:] Dunne et al. [] attempted to measure acuity colour discrimination and visual contrast; however, none of the participants could complete the assessments.
claims.location: Dunne 2004 Abstract (Methods, Results); Gaffney 2026 full text section 4.2
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 9 men, advanced Alzheimer's disease, long-term care, USA. I: high-contrast red tableware (10 days). C: white tableware before and after (10 days each). O: grams of food, ounces of liquid at lunch and supper. T: 30 days.
claims.safe_wording: In a 2004 study, nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease living in long-term care ate about a quarter more food and drank much more (84% more on average) during 10 days with high-contrast red plates and cups than during 10 days with white ones. Eight of the nine ate or drank more.
claims.qualifications: Nine men only; no randomisation (white, then red, then white, the same men throughout); 10 days per condition; relative increases in average intake, not absolute amounts; no weight or health outcomes. Do not call it 'the best-known study' (not verifiable); say it is the study that tested red tableware, or 'a 2004 study of nine men'. Do not say 'one facility' (not confirmed in the abstract); say 'in long-term care'. PubMed labels it an RCT, but the design is before-during-after.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C13-33-d (Donnelly: blue plates did not clearly increase intake). Vision was not measurable in any participant, so the mechanism is inferred.

numbers.meaning: participants, all men with advanced Alzheimer's disease
per condition (white, red, white); 30 days in total, two meals a day
mean relative increase in food intake (grams), red versus white baseline
mean relative increase in liquid intake (ounces), red versus white baseline
participants whose intake increased

claims.claim: In a follow-up a year later, high-contrast blue tableware also increased intake, while low-contrast red and low-contrast blue did not, which points to contrast rather than the colour red.
claims.supporting_passage: In a follow-up study 1 year later, other contrast conditions were examined (high-contrast blue, low-contrast red and low-contrast blue). ... In the follow-up study, the high-contrast intervention (blue) resulted in significant increases in food and liquid intake; the low-contrast red and low-contrast blue interventions were ineffectual. [Gaffney 2026:] In a follow-up study a year later, they used high-contrast blue tableware with low-contrast (pastel) red and low-contrast blue tableware [].
claims.location: Dunne 2004 Abstract (Methods, Results); Gaffney 2026 full text section 3.5
claims.pico_timeframe: Same research group and setting, 1 year later; high-contrast blue versus low-contrast (pastel) red and low-contrast blue tableware; food and liquid intake.
claims.safe_wording: A year later the same team tried other plates. Strongly contrasting blue plates also increased eating and drinking; pale red and pale blue plates did not. That points to contrast between food and plate, not to redness.
claims.qualifications: Same small study; the abstract does not give the number of participants in the follow-up or confirm they were the same men. Say 'points to', not 'shows'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Donnelly (in Gaffney 2026) found no significant improvement with blue versus white dishware when meals included low-contrast foods; Gaffney notes 'no strong consensus on which specific colours or tableware types are most effective'.

numbers.meaning: interval between the original study and the follow-up

claims.claim: A 2026 systematic review found only four small studies of visual contrast at meals (64 participants in all), none randomised, and judged the evidence limited, low quality and inconclusive; it is not established that high-contrast tableware improves nutrition.
claims.supporting_passage: Of 2901 records screened, four studies (five reports) met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 64 participants. ... Limited and low-quality evidence suggests a possible effect of modifying the dining environment to improve visual contrast for enhancing dietary intake in older adults, with visual contrast sensitivity, particularly those with dementia. However, the evidence gap is large and remains inconclusive. [Full text:] A total of 64 participants were included across the studies; sample sizes were small, ranging from 9 to 25. ... The studies consisted of mixed methods (= 1) and non-randomised quantitative designs (= 4). ... with the longest test period lasting 30 days. ... MMAT scores ranged from 40 to 60%. ... this review has identified a clear evidence gap instead of establishing the effectiveness of visual contrast interventions. ... Although the studies included in this review have demonstrated increases in food intakes, it remains unclear whether these translate to meaningful outcomes in the long term, such as reduced prevalence of malnutrition, reduced unintentional weight loss, or optimised nutritional status among older adults in long-term aged care.
claims.location: Gaffney 2026 Abstract; full text sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 4 and 4.3
claims.pico_timeframe: P: adults 65+ (in practice, long-term care residents with dementia). I: visual contrast (tableware, tablecloths, lighting). C: usual tableware or baseline. O: food or fluid intake; weight/malnutrition not reported. T: longest 30 days. Search to March 2025.
claims.safe_wording: A 2026 review of all the studies it could find on contrast at mealtimes found four, with 64 people in total, the largest with 25. None was randomised and none lasted more than a month. The reviewers called the evidence limited, low quality and inconclusive, and none of the studies showed whether contrast plates prevent weight loss or malnutrition.
claims.qualifications: An evidence gap is not evidence of no effect: most studies reported more eating, though statistical significance varied. Do not say contrast plates 'don't work'. 'Harmless' or 'no downside' is not established by any source here; if used, frame as judgement (for example 'cheap to try').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The review's authors see 'a possible effect' and call a 25% increase clinically important despite n=9; the uncertainty is about size and durability, not direction alone.

numbers.meaning: all studies meeting inclusion criteria to March 2025
participants across all four studies
range of study sizes
longest test period in any included study
MMAT quality scores (higher is better, maximum 100%)

claims.claim: Another study of blue versus white dishware in people with dementia did not show a clear increase in food intake.
claims.supporting_passage: In comparison, Donnelly et al. [] reported that the average number of participant observations was 19 ± 2 meals and found that only less than a third (28%) of participants increased intake by at least 10% during the intervention periods when blue tableware was used. ... Donnelly et al. [] challenged this, finding no significant improvement in food intake with blue dishware compared to white in meals containing low-contrast foods, like mashed potato and white rice, indicating that colour alone may not be sufficient to improve dietary intake.
claims.pico_timeframe: Donnelly et al. (as reported in the review; primary paper not opened): 18 people with dementia, crossover blue versus white dishware, menu with more low-contrast foods; food intake.
claims.safe_wording: A later study of blue plates in 18 people with dementia did not find a clear increase in eating; fewer than a third ate at least a tenth more.
claims.qualifications: Reported via the systematic review; the Donnelly primary paper was not opened. Use as the result that went the other way, stated as plainly as the Dunne headline.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small study; not statistically significant, which is not proof of no effect.

numbers.meaning: participants in Donnelly who increased intake by at least 10% with blue tableware
participants with dementia in Donnelly (per Gaffney: 'Donnelly had double the participants (= 18, five males)')

claims.claim: More broadly, systematic reviews have not established any specific mealtime environment change, or form of eating assistance, as effective for people with dementia.
claims.supporting_passage: [Herke 2018:] We included nine studies, investigating 1502 people. ... The overall quality of evidence was mainly low to very low. ... Due to the quantity and quality of the evidence currently available, we cannot identify any specific environmental or behavioural modifications for improving food and fluid intake in people with dementia. [Abdelhamid 2016:] Forty-three controlled interventions were included, disappointingly none were judged at low risk of bias. ... Eating assistance studies provided inconsistent evidence ... We found no definitive evidence on effectiveness, or lack of effectiveness, of specific interventions but studies were small and short term.
claims.location: Herke 2018 Abstract (Main results, Authors' conclusions); Abdelhamid 2016 Abstract (Results, Conclusions)
claims.pico_timeframe: People with dementia or cognitive impairment, all settings; environmental, behavioural and direct eating-support interventions; food and fluid intake and nutritional status.
claims.safe_wording: Reviews of mealtime changes for people with dementia have not found any single change that is proven to help people eat more, including help with eating, because the studies are small and short.
claims.qualifications: This cuts both ways: the post's position that plates should not replace help with eating must be stated as judgement ('We should not count a plate in place of a person'), not as a finding that eating assistance is proven in dementia. Simmons 2008 (C13-36-c/d; 41 to 43% had dementia) is the nearest trial evidence that one-to-one help increases intake in nursing home residents.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Herke searched to January 2018 and included RCTs only.

numbers.meaning: Herke 2018 Cochrane review
controlled interventions in Abdelhamid 2016; none at low risk of bias

claims.claim: Of 40 well older people (over 65) tested on packs routinely used in NSW hospitals, 39% could not open cheese portions and 10% could not open water bottles; tetra packs, water bottles, cereal, fruit cups, desserts, biscuits and cheese portions were the hardest.
claims.supporting_passage: The aim of this paper was to assess the ability of well older people living in the community to open food and beverage items routinely used in NSW hospitals ... A sample of 40 older people in good health aged over 65 years from 3 community settings participated in the study. ... Tetra packs, water bottles, cereal, fruit cups, desserts, biscuits and cheese portions appeared to be the most difficult food products to open. Ten percent of the sample could not open the water bottles and 39% could not open cheese portions.
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 40 healthy community-dwelling people over 65, NSW, Australia. Exposure: packs used in NSW hospitals. O: observed success at opening, time, grip and pinch strength. Single testing session.
claims.safe_wording: In an Australian study, about 4 in 10 healthy people over 65 could not open a hospital cheese portion, and 1 in 10 could not open a bottle of water. They were well volunteers, not patients.
claims.qualifications: Well volunteers living at home, not inpatients (people who are ill are likely to find it harder, but that is inference). Australian hospital packaging; UK packs may differ and no UK study was found in this search.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; results consistent with Bell 2013 inpatient data.

numbers.meaning: healthy people over 65 from 3 community settings
of the 40 could not open cheese portions (about 4 in 10)
of the 40 could not open water bottles (1 in 10)

claims.claim: Among 140 mostly older inpatients in four Australian public hospitals, several common packs were found difficult to open by at least 40% of patients, including milk and juices (52%) and cereal (49%).
claims.supporting_passage: Participants (140 mostly elderly inpatients and 64 staff members) were recruited from four local public hospitals. ... Several food and beverage packages were found difficult to open by at least 40% of patients. These included milk and juices (52%), cereal (49%), condiments (46%), tetra packs (40%) and water bottles (40%). The difficulties were attributed to 'fiddly' packaging, hand strength and vision;
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 140 mostly older inpatients, 4 public hospitals, Illawarra, NSW, Australia. Exposure: hospital food and drink packaging. O: reported/observed difficulty opening. Cross-sectional, about 2012.
claims.safe_wording: In four Australian hospitals, about half of 140 mostly older patients found milk, juice and cereal packs difficult to open.
claims.qualifications: 'Found difficult to open', not 'could not open'. 'Mostly elderly' inpatients, not all over 65. Australian packaging, about 2012. This is the original of the 'earlier research' mentioned in the Bell 2016 abstract; cite it directly rather than via Bell 2016's background.

numbers.meaning: mostly older inpatients in 4 public hospitals
of patients found milk and juices difficult to open
of patients found cereal difficult to open
condiments
tetra packs; also water bottles

claims.claim: Opening hospital packs lying in a hospital bed needed more pinch strength and finger dexterity than sitting in a chair; the authors conclude that sitting to eat helps with opening packs.
claims.supporting_passage: the present laboratory study examined the differences between participants opening a selection of products in a hospital bed and a chair. ... in a sample of well older community dwelling adults (n = 34). ... Honey sachets, cheese portions, foil sealed thickened pudding and tetra packs were the most difficult packs to open, with 15% of cheese portions unable to be opened in either the bed or chair posture. Although grip strength was consistent for each posture, pinch grips and dexterity were adversely affected by the bed posture. Lying in a hospital bed required greater pinch strength and dexterity to open packs. ... The present study demonstrates that eating in a seated posture is also advantageous for opening the food and beverage packs used in the NSW hospital food service and supports the notion that patients should sit to eat in hospital.
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 34 healthy community-dwelling older adults, NSW. I: opening packs in a hospital bed. C: opening packs in a chair. O: grip and pinch strength, dexterity, time, attempts, satisfaction. Laboratory, single session.
claims.safe_wording: In a laboratory test with 34 healthy older volunteers, opening packs while lying in a hospital bed took more finger strength and more nimble fingers than opening them sitting in a chair. The researchers concluded that patients should sit up to eat.
claims.qualifications: The abstract does not report how many more packs were opened sitting than lying; do not claim a success-rate difference. Avoid the '15%' figure, whose denominator (cheese portions attempted, per posture or combined) is unclear. The line 'eating in a seated position when in hospital has been shown to improve intake' is the authors' background statement, not this study's finding; do not use it as a finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small laboratory study in well volunteers.

numbers.meaning: healthy community-dwelling older adults tested in both bed and chair

claims.claim: The packaging studies are Australian (New South Wales) and mostly in well volunteers; packaging in UK hospitals may differ; recording unopened food as 'not accessible' rather than 'refused' is a judgement.
claims.supporting_passage: The aim of this paper was to assess the ability of well older people living in the community to open food and beverage items routinely used in NSW hospitals [Bell 2016]. ... Participants (140 mostly elderly inpatients and 64 staff members) were recruited from four local public hospitals. [Bell 2013; study conducted in the Illawarra region of NSW, Australia]
claims.pico_timeframe: Setting limitation for all three packaging studies.
claims.safe_wording: These studies were done in Australia, mostly with healthy volunteers. Packs in UK hospitals may differ, but the same kinds of portion packs are common.
claims.qualifications: The final clause ('same kinds of portion packs are common') is not sourced; omit it or mark it as observation. The action (open the packets, help the person sit up, record unopened food as not accessible) is a judgement and should read as advice, not as a trial finding; no study here tested whether opening packets increases intake.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No UK study of pack opening by older inpatients was found in a PubMed search in this batch.

claims.claim: In 74 residents of three US nursing homes given a two-day, six-meal trial of one-to-one feeding assistance, half significantly increased their food and fluid intake at meals.
claims.supporting_passage: Seventy-four residents in three NHs received a 2-day, or six-meal, trial of one-on-one feeding assistance. Total percentage (0% to 100%) of food and fluid consumed during mealtime was estimated across 3 days during usual NH care and 2 days during the intervention. ... One half (50%) of the participants significantly increased their oral food and fluid intake during mealtime.
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 74 residents, 3 US nursing homes. I: one-to-one feeding assistance for 2 days (6 meals). C: 3 days of usual care in the same residents. O: estimated percent of food and fluid consumed. T: 5 days.
claims.safe_wording: In a 2001 US study of 74 nursing home residents, half ate and drank significantly more at meals during two days of one-to-one help.
claims.qualifications: Keep 'significantly'; the other half did not show a significant increase. Two days only, no control group, no weight outcome, US 2001.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Abdelhamid 2016 found eating assistance studies in dementia gave inconsistent evidence.

numbers.meaning: residents in 3 US nursing homes
of the 74 significantly increased mealtime food and fluid intake (half)
length of the assistance trial

claims.claim: The one-to-one help took an average of 38 minutes per resident per meal, compared with 9 minutes of help given by nursing home staff in usual care; the help was given by research staff.
claims.supporting_passage: [Simmons 2001:] The intervention required significantly more staff time to implement (average of 38 minutes per resident/meal vs 9 minutes rendered by NH staff). ... These data suggest that it will almost certainly be necessary to both increase staffing levels and to organize staff better to produce higher quality feeding assistance during mealtimes. [Simmons 2008, Introduction, describing the group's earlier two-day studies:] These feeding assistance interventions required a significant increase in staff time from an average of less than 10 minutes to 35 minutes per resident per meal and one minute or less to 12 minutes per resident per snack. In these studies, research staff implemented the interventions for only a two-day period to determine the immediate effect of the interventions on residents’ oral food and fluid intake.
claims.location: Simmons 2001 Abstract (Results, Conclusions); Simmons 2008 full text, Introduction
claims.pico_timeframe: As C13-36-a. Timed observation of assistance per resident per meal under usual care and under the intervention.
claims.safe_wording: The help took an average of 38 minutes per resident per meal. In usual care, nursing home staff gave about 9 minutes. The help in the study was given by the research team, not the home's own staff.
claims.qualifications: The research-staff point comes from the same authors' 2008 paper describing their earlier two-day studies (the 2001 PDF could not be opened); the 2001 abstract itself contrasts the 38 minutes with '9 minutes rendered by NH staff'. The 2008 introduction pools the earlier studies as 'less than 10 minutes to 35 minutes'; use the 2001 abstract figures (38 and 9) when citing the 2001 study, and do not mix the two.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the direction; exact minutes vary between studies (35, 38, 42).

numbers.meaning: average one-to-one assistance time per resident per meal (intervention, 2001)
average assistance time per resident per meal given by nursing home staff in usual care (2001)

claims.claim: In a later controlled trial (2008) in four US nursing homes, mealtime help given by trained research staff took an average of 42 minutes per person per meal, against about 5 minutes of help in usual care.
claims.supporting_passage: [Abstract:] Seventy-six long-stay NH residents at risk for unintentional weight loss. ... Research staff provided feeding assistance twice per day during or between meals, 5 days per week for 24 weeks. ... The average amount of staff time required to provide the interventions was 42 minutes per person per meal and 13 minutes per person per between-meal snack, versus usual care, during which residents received, on average, 5 minutes of assistance per person per meal and less than 1 minute per person per snack. [Results:] Research staff spent an average of 42.19 (± 19.05) minutes per person per meal providing mealtime assistance. Most often (87% of care episodes), assistance was provided one-to-one; ... The average amount of NH staff time spent providing assistance to eat during meals to residents in the control group showed no significant change during the initial 24-week or crossover phases (average < 10 minutes per person per meal at each measurement point for all meals).
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 76 long-stay residents with low intake, at risk of weight loss, 4 US nursing homes; mean age 82 to 83; MMSE 15; 41 to 43% dementia diagnosis. I: mealtime assistance or between-meal snacks by trained research staff, twice a day, 5 days a week. C: usual care (crossover). T: 24 weeks each phase.
claims.safe_wording: A later US trial found the same thing. Trained research staff took an average of 42 minutes per person to help with a meal, mostly one-to-one. In usual care, residents got about 5 minutes of help per meal.
claims.qualifications: The 42 minutes comes from the 19 residents who received mealtime help. Usual care: the abstract gives 5 minutes on average; results say under 10 minutes at every measurement; use 'about 5 minutes' or 'under 10 minutes', not both as separate figures. US, 2008, one region.

claims.claim: In the 2008 trial, residents gained weight relative to usual care during the feeding-assistance periods, but most of the gain came from between-meal snacks, not mealtime help.
claims.supporting_passage: The intervention group experienced a 0.72 unit gain in final BMI value (. Model 1) and a 4-pound gain in final body weight (. Model 3) relative to the control group. ... Overall, 56% of participants maintained or gained weight during intervention compared to 28% during control. ... Of the 76 unique participants who completed intervention, 19 (25%) received mealtime assistance and 57 (75%) received snacks; thus, most of the gain in estimated total daily calories for the intervention group was due to snacks.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C13-36-c; weight measured monthly by research staff over 24-week phases.
claims.safe_wording: With this extra help, 56 in 100 residents kept or gained weight, against 28 in 100 in usual care. Most of that came from snacks offered between meals rather than from help at meals.
claims.qualifications: Do not attribute the weight result to the 42-minute mealtime help. 4 lb is about 1.8 kg (relative to control). Help given by research staff; the authors say it is unknown whether the homes' own staff could sustain it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small crossover trial randomised by facility (4 homes).

claims.claim: In the 2008 trial homes, day-shift staffing was 6 to 11 residents per nurse aide, and the authors state that most US nursing homes lack the nurse aide staffing to give feeding assistance to all residents who need it.
claims.supporting_passage: [Simmons 2008 Methods:] Nurse-aide level staff-to-resident ratios across the four NHs, as reported by the directors-of-nursing, ranged from 6 to 11 residents per nurse aide on the 7am to 3pm shift and 11 to 15 residents per nurse aide on the 3pm to 11pm shift. [Discussion:] Given that most U.S. NHs do not have adequate nurse aide staffing to provide feeding assistance for all residents in need, it may be more feasible in daily care practice to group residents at risk for unintentional weight loss for snack delivery at least twice daily. ... Finally, the interventions were provided by research staff. It is unknown if indigenous NH staff could maintain these interventions with sufficient consistency in daily care practice to have the same effects on residents’ oral intake, weight and BMI status.
claims.location: Simmons 2008 full text, Methods (Setting) and Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Four US nursing homes, about 2005 to 2007; staffing ratios reported by directors of nursing.
claims.safe_wording: In the homes in that trial, one care aide on the day shift looked after 6 to 11 residents. The researchers wrote that most US nursing homes do not have enough aides to give this help to everyone who needs it.
claims.qualifications: Do not multiply ratios by minutes to state a shortfall as a finding (not every resident needs help); if a worked example is used, label it 'Illustrative example'. US staffing from about 2008; UK wards and care homes may differ and no UK figure was found. The position that staffing should be planned from the minutes help takes is judgement, consistent with the authors' 2001 conclusion ('it will almost certainly be necessary to both increase staffing levels and to organize staff better').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The authors also suggest grouping residents and snack rounds as more feasible; the post should not imply one-to-one help at every meal is the only answer.

numbers.meaning: residents per nurse aide on the 7am to 3pm shift in the four trial homes
residents per nurse aide on the 3pm to 11pm shift

claims.claim: In five Dutch nursing homes, 178 residents without dementia (mean age 77) were cluster randomised by ward to family style meals or usual pre-plated service for six months.
claims.supporting_passage: [Abstract:] To assess the effect of family style mealtimes on quality of life, physical performance, and body weight of nursing home residents without dementia. ... Five Dutch nursing homes. 178 residents (mean age 77 years). Two wards in each home were randomised to intervention (95 participants) or control groups (83). During six months the intervention group took their meals family style and the control group received the usual individual pre-plated service. [Full text, Methods:] In most Dutch nursing homes two types of care are available: psychogeriatric care for residents with dementia or chronic somatic care for patients with conditions such as stroke or Parkinson’s disease. ... We excluded residents in the terminal phase of disease, those needing total parenteral feeding, and those unable to give informed consent owing to a physical or mental condition.
claims.location: Nijs 2006 Abstract; full text Methods (Participants and study design)
claims.pico_timeframe: P: 178 residents of chronic somatic wards (e.g. stroke, Parkinson's disease), no dementia, mean age 77, 5 Dutch nursing homes. I: family style mealtimes (95). C: usual pre-plated service (83). O: quality of life, motor function, body weight, energy intake. T: 6 months.
claims.safe_wording: A Dutch trial in five nursing homes randomly assigned wards to family style meals or the usual plated meals for six months. The 178 residents did not have dementia; many had conditions such as stroke or Parkinson's disease.
claims.qualifications: State early that residents did not have dementia (judge's instruction). Randomised by ward (10 wards), not by person. 2006, Netherlands, nursing homes; hospital wards were not studied.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Single trial; no replication found in this batch.

claims.claim: Compared with plated meals, family style meals led to better quality of life, fine motor function and body weight over six months: quality of life stayed stable with family style meals and fell with plated meals, and weight stayed stable with family style meals and fell by about 1 kg with plated meals (difference 1.5 kg).
claims.supporting_passage: [Abstract:] The difference in change between the groups was significant for overall quality of life (6.1 units, 95% confidence interval 2.1 to 10.3), fine motor function (1.8 units, 0.6 to 3.0), and body weight (1.5 kg, 0.6 to 2.4). [Full text, Methods:] The questionnaire consists of 50 statements, scored on a dichotomous scale (yes or no). Each subscale and the total questionnaire could be computed to a range of 0 to 100 ... A high score represents a high quality of life. [Results:] The difference in changes in quality of life between both groups was significant (6.1 units, 95% confidence interval 2.1 to 10.3 units; table 3). The intervention group remained stable (0.4, − 1.8 to 2.5) whereas the control group declined ( − 5.0, − 9.4 to − 0.6). ... Mean body weight remained relatively stable in the intervention group (0.5 kg, − 0.3 to 1.2 kg) but decreased significantly in the control group ( − 1.1, − 1.9 to − 0.2). Changes in body weight between control and intervention groups were significantly different (1.5, 0.6 to 2.4). ... Mean energy intake increased significantly in the intervention group (481 kJ, 84 to 878 kJ) but decreased significantly in the control group ( − 420, − 713 to − 127). Changes in energy intake between control and intervention group were significantly different (991, 504 to 1479).
claims.location: Nijs 2006 Abstract; full text Methods (Quality of life) and Results
claims.pico_timeframe: As C13-32-a. Quality of life by face-to-face interview, Dutch quality of life of somatic nursing home residents questionnaire (0 to 100). Change from baseline to 6 months.
claims.safe_wording: Over six months, residents who ate family style held their weight steady, while those given plated meals lost about 1 kg; the gap between groups was 1.5 kg. Quality of life scores held steady with family style meals but fell with plated meals. Residents eating family style also ate more.
claims.qualifications: The advantage is mostly that the plated group got worse; say 'held steady' rather than 'improved'. For the public, avoid '6.1 units'; if used for practitioners, say '6 points on a 0 to 100 scale'. Do not convert the energy figures to calories unless the time unit (per day) is confirmed; say 'ate more'. Causal wording ('led to') is acceptable for this randomised comparison, but it applies to the whole package (see C13-32-c).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Only 10 clusters; single trial; not replicated in this batch.

claims.claim: Family style mealtimes in the trial were a package: tablecloths and proper crockery, cooked food served in dishes on the table with choice, most residents serving themselves, staff sitting and chatting at each table, and no interruptions during meals.
claims.supporting_passage: [Table 1, Family style mealtimes:] Table dressing: Tablecloth; drinking glasses (no plastic cups); normal plates; full cutlery; napkins; subtle flower arrangements. Food services: Cooked meal served in dishes on table; menu choice between two types of vegetables, meat, and staple foods; no ready to eat sandwiches during breakfast or supper. Staff protocol: Staff sit down at tables and chat with residents; minimum of one nurse or nutrition assistant or volunteer per table; drugs handed out before start of meal; no change of staff during mealtimes ... Residents’ protocol: Balanced seating of residents (typically six per table); residents decide when food is served; most residents serve themselves, with some help from nurse or table companion; mealtimes begin when everybody is seated ... Mealtime protocol: No other activities (for example, cleaning, visits from doctor); dining room closed for visitors and healthcare providers (except where observation by healthcare giver is necessary or visitors help residents) ...
claims.location: Nijs 2006 full text, Methods (The intervention) and Table 1
claims.pico_timeframe: Description of the intervention delivered for 6 months.
claims.safe_wording: Family style meant more than shared dishes. Tables had cloths, glasses and proper plates. Food came in dishes and most residents served themselves. A member of staff sat and chatted at every table, and nothing else happened in the dining room during the meal.
claims.qualifications: The trial cannot say which part helped; do not credit self-service alone. The candidate's opening ('served themselves from shared dishes') must mention that staff sat at the table. Table 1 also lists a moment for reflection or prayer before eating; house style bans religious references, so leave it out rather than misdescribe it (the list above is a faithful partial description).

numbers.meaning: residents per table, with at least one staff member or volunteer per table

claims.claim: For people with dementia, family style meals are listed as promising in a systematic review, but the evidence is small and not definitive.
claims.supporting_passage: [Bunn 2016:] We included 56 interventions (reported in 51 studies). Studies were small and there were no clearly effective, or clearly ineffective, interventions. Promising interventions included: eating meals with care-givers, family style meals, soothing mealtime music, constantly accessible snacks and longer mealtimes, ... We found no definitive evidence on effectiveness, or lack of effectiveness, of specific interventions but studies were small and short term. [Nijs 2006, Discussion:] Earlier research showed that residents with dementia benefit from these kinds of interventions. Although we excluded this important group, we think that our principal conclusion may be extended to all nursing home residents.
claims.location: Bunn 2016 Abstract (Results, Conclusions); Nijs 2006 full text, Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: People with cognitive impairment or dementia, all settings; indirect interventions including family style meals; food and drink intake.
claims.safe_wording: For people with dementia, a review of the studies lists family style meals as promising, but the studies are small and short, so the benefit is not proven.
claims.qualifications: Nijs's view that the result may extend to all residents is the authors' opinion, not a finding. Do not say family style meals 'work' in dementia.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Herke 2018 Cochrane (RCTs only) could not identify any specific environmental or behavioural modification for food intake in dementia.

numbers.meaning: Bunn 2016 indirect-interventions review

candidates.reason: All essential claims supported. Dunne 2004 abstract confirms 9 men with advanced Alzheimer's in long-term care, 10 days per condition, +25% food and +84% liquid (relative, mean) with high-contrast red versus white, 8 of 9 increased, and a follow-up where high-contrast blue worked and low-contrast red and blue did not. The judge's requirement for a systematic review is met by a better source than Abdelhamid: Gaffney 2026 (Nutrients; full text read) found only 4 studies, 64 participants (9 to 25 each), none randomised, longest 30 days, MMAT 40 to 60%, and called the evidence limited, low quality and inconclusive, with no long-term nutritional outcomes. The result that went the other way (Donnelly: blue versus white, no significant increase; 28% ate at least 10% more) must be stated. Wording required: 'points to contrast rather than redness', not 'the finding is about contrast'; not 'best-known study' or 'one facility' (unverified); 'not established' or 'unproven', never 'does not work'; 'harmless' is unsourced, so frame as judgement or say 'cheap to try'. The claim that plates should not replace help with eating is judgement: reviews also find eating assistance in dementia unproven (Abdelhamid 2016; Herke 2018), though Simmons 2008 shows one-to-one help increases intake in nursing home residents (41 to 43% with dementia).

Supported from three abstracts. Bell 2016: of 40 healthy people over 65, 39% could not open cheese portions and 10% could not open water bottles (about 4 in 10; 1 in 10). The 'earlier research' is now sourced from the original Bell 2013 (140 mostly older inpatients, 4 NSW hospitals): at least 40% found several packs difficult, including milk and juices 52% and cereal 49%. Using this strengthens the post because it is real patients, but its outcome is 'found difficult', not 'could not open'. Bell 2017 (34 well volunteers, laboratory): opening packs in a hospital bed needed more pinch strength and dexterity than in a chair, and the authors conclude patients should sit to eat. The abstract gives no success-rate difference, and the '15%' figure has an unclear denominator, so leave both out. Label the populations as described (well Australian volunteers; mostly older Australian inpatients); UK packs may differ and no UK study was found. 'Record unopened food as not accessible' is judgement, and no study tested whether opening packets raises intake.

Simmons 2001 abstract supports 74 residents, 3 US homes, a 2-day six-meal trial, half significantly increased intake, 38 versus 9 minutes per resident per meal. Who delivered the help: the 2001 PDF could not be opened. The same authors' 2008 paper states that research staff delivered the earlier two-day interventions, and the 2001 abstract contrasts the help with '9 minutes rendered by NH staff'. As the judge asked, a more recent and stronger figure was added. Simmons 2008 (crossover controlled trial, 76 residents, 4 US homes, 24 weeks; full text read) found trained research staff took 42 minutes per person per meal, 87% of episodes one-to-one, against about 5 minutes (under 10) in usual care. Also 56% versus 28% kept or gained weight, but only 19 of 76 got mealtime help and most of the calorie gain came from snacks, so the weight result must not be credited to mealtime help. Day-shift ratios in those homes were 6 to 11 residents per aide, and the authors state most US homes lack the aide staffing for this help. Do not compute a shortfall from ratios times minutes except as a labelled illustration. No UK figure was found; state as a limitation. The line 'care workers are not failing; the plan is' is judgement and fits the values brief.

Nijs 2006 was read in full through Undermind, since PMC returned no body. The design is confirmed: 178 residents without dementia (chronic somatic wards, e.g. stroke, Parkinson's), mean age 77, 5 Dutch homes, ward-level randomisation, 6 months. The plain meaning the judge asked for is available. Quality of life (0 to 100 scale) stayed stable with family style meals (+0.4) and fell with plated meals (-5.0), a difference of 6.1. Weight stayed stable (+0.5 kg) against a 1.1 kg loss, a difference of 1.5 kg. Energy intake rose with family style meals and fell with plated meals. Two framing requirements. First, the benefit is mostly the plated group getting worse, so say 'held steady'. Second, the intervention was a package (tablecloths and proper crockery, dishes on the table with choice, self-service, staff sitting and chatting at each table, no interruptions), so the opening must not credit self-service alone. The dementia limitation is sourced: Bunn 2016 (EDWINA) lists family style meals as promising but not proven in dementia. Nursing homes only; hospital wards were not studied. Leave out the trial's pre-meal reflection or prayer element (house style).
